text: The Network Repository Function (NRF) is the logical function that provides discovery and registration services for all Network Functions (NFs) and Service Communication Proxies (SCPs) in the 5G Core. It maintains the NF and SCP profiles, including their supported services and health status, and enables other NFs or SCPs to discover the instances and service endpoints they need (TS 23.501, §6.3.1). Through the NF‑Discovery procedure, the NRF receives discovery requests and returns the information of the discovered NF instances (TS 23.501, §6.2.6.1). It also receives NF registration messages (e.g., Nnrf_NFManagement_NFRegister) so that newly operative NF instances become discoverable, and it notifies subscribed consumers about newly registered, updated, or deregistered NF/SCP instances (TS 23.501, §6.2.6.1).

The Access and Mobility Management Function (AMF) provides the following main functions【TS 23.501, §6.2.1】:

- Termination of the RAN control‑plane interface (N2)  
- Termination of the NAS interface (N1) together with NAS ciphering and integrity protection  
- Registration management  
- Connection management  
- Reachability management  
- Mobility management  
- Lawful intercept for AMF events and the interface to the lawful‑intercept system  
- Transport of SM (Session Management) messages between the UE and the SMF, acting as a transparent proxy for routing those messages  
- Access authentication and access authorization  
- Transport of SMS messages between the UE and the SMSF  
- Security Anchor Functionality (SEAF) as defined in TS 33.501  
- Location Services management for regulatory services and transport of Location Services messages between the UE, LMF and the RAN  
- EPS Bearer ID allocation for interworking with EPS  
- UE mobility‑event notification  
- S‑NSSAI per‑TA mapping notification  
- Support for Control‑Plane CIoT 5GS optimisation  
- Support for User‑Plane CIoT 5GS optimisation  
- Support for restriction of use of Enhanced Coverage  
- Provisioning of external parameters (Expected UE Behaviour parameters or Network Configuration parameters)  
- Support for Network‑Slice‑specific authentication and authorization  
- Support for charging  
- Control of 5G access‑stratum‑based time distribution based on the UE’s subscription data  
- Control of the gNB’s time‑synchronisation status reporting and subscription【TS 23.501, §6.2.1】.

The UPF provides a wide range of user‑plane and control‑plane functions, including:

- Anchor point for intra‑/inter‑RAT mobility (when applicable) (TS 23.501, §6.2.3)  
- Allocation of UE IP address/prefix in response to SMF request (TS 23.501, §6.2.3)  
- External PDU Session point of interconnect to the Data Network (TS 23.501, §6.2.3)  
- Packet routing and forwarding (e.g., uplink classifier, branching point for multi‑homed PDU Sessions, forwarding within a 5G VN group) (TS 23.501, §6.2.3)  
- Packet inspection (application detection based on service data flow templates and optional PFDs) (TS 23.501, §6.2.3)  
- User‑plane part of policy‑rule enforcement (gating, redirection, traffic steering) (TS 23.501, §6.2.3)  
- Lawful intercept (UP collection) (TS 23.501, §6.2.3)  
- Traffic‑usage reporting (TS 23.501, §6.2.3)  
- QoS handling for the user plane (uplink/downlink rate enforcement, Reflective QoS marking) (TS 23.501, §6.2.3)  
- Uplink traffic verification (SDF to QoS Flow mapping) (TS 23.501, §6.2.3)  
- Transport‑level packet marking in uplink and downlink (TS 23.501, §6.2.3)  
- Downlink packet buffering and downlink‑data‑notification triggering (TS 23.501, §6.2.3)  
- Sending and forwarding of one or more “end marker” packets to the source NG‑RAN node (TS 23.501, §6.2.3)  
- Responding to ARP and IPv6 Neighbor‑Solicitation requests based on local cache (TS 23.501, §6.2.3)  
- Packet duplication in downlink and elimination in uplink at the GTP‑U layer (TS 23.501, §6.2.3)  
- Network‑time‑triggered (NW‑TT) functionality (TS 23.501, §6.2.3)  
- High‑latency communication support (TS 23.501, §6.2.3)  
- ATSSS steering functionality to steer MA PDU Session traffic (TS 23.501, §6.2.3)  
- Inter‑PLMN UP Security (IPUPS) functionality (TS 23.501, §6.2.3)  
- Event exposure (QoS monitoring, analytics, TSC management) (TS 23.501, §6.2.3)  
- Exposure of UE information (e.g., UE IP address translation when NAT is deployed) (TS 23.501, §6.2.3)  
- Support for PDU‑Set‑based handling (TS 23.501, §6.2.3)
The N4 reference point connects the **SMF (Session Management Function)** and the **UPF (User Plane Function)** (TS 23.501, §4.2.7).

A 5QI (5G QoS Identifier) is a scalar value that serves as a reference to the 5G QoS characteristics defined in clause 5.7.4; these characteristics include access‑node‑specific parameters that control QoS forwarding treatment for a QoS Flow (e.g., scheduling weights, admission thresholds, queue‑management thresholds, link‑layer protocol configuration, etc.) (TS 23.501, §5.7.2.1).

An S‑NSSAI consists of a Slice/Service Type (SST) and, optionally, a Slice Differentiator (SD) — the SST identifies the expected network‑slice behaviour, while the SD (when present) further distinguishes among multiple slices of the same SST (TS 23.501, §5.15.2.1).

The 5G System defines three Session and Service Continuity (SSC) modes for a PDU Session:

* **SSC mode 1** – the network preserves the connectivity service (the IP address is retained for IPv4/IPv6/IPv4v6 sessions)【TS 23.501, §5.6.9.1】.  
* **SSC mode 2** – the network may release the connectivity service and the associated PDU Session, causing the allocated IP address(es) to be released【TS 23.501, §5.6.9.1】.  
* **SSC mode 3** – the network establishes a new PDU Session Anchor before releasing the previous one, allowing a change of the user‑plane without loss of connectivity (the IP address is not preserved when the anchor changes)【TS 23.501, §5.6.9.1】.

The Network Slice Selection Function (NSSF) performs the following functions:

* Selects the set of Network Slice instances that will serve the UE. (TS 23.501, §6.2.14)  
* Determines the **Allowed NSSAI** and, when required, maps it to the UE’s **Subscribed S‑NSSAIs**. (TS 23.501, §6.2.14)  
* Determines the **Configured NSSAI** and, when required, maps it to the UE’s **Subscribed S‑NSSAIs**. (TS 23.501, §6.2.14)  
* Determines the AMF Set (or, based on configuration, a list of candidate AMFs) that shall serve the UE, possibly after querying the NRF. (TS 23.501, §6.2.14)  
* May provide support for Network Slice restriction and Network Slice instance restriction using NWDAF analytics. (TS 23.501, §6.2.14)  
* Determines whether an S‑NSSAI has to be replaced and, if so, indicates to the AMF that the S‑NSSAI is unavailable and supplies an **Alternative S‑NSSAI** (e.g., based on NWDAF analytics or an OAM trigger). (TS 23.501, §6.2.14)  

In addition, during registration to a set of network slices the NSSF:

* Verifies which S‑NSSAIs in the Requested NSSAI are permitted by comparing them with the Subscribed S‑NSSAIs and the mapping to HPLMN S‑NSSAIs, and applies default S‑NSSAIs when no Requested NSSAI is provided or none are permitted. (TS 23.501, §5.15.5.2.1)  
* May use NWDAF analytics (slice load level, observed service experience, dispersion analytics) to determine the list of S‑NSSAIs in the Allowed NSSAI when the AMF has not subscribed to slice‑availability notifications. (TS 23.501, §5.15.5.2.1)  
* Selects the Network Slice instance(s) that will serve the UE; if multiple instances can serve a given S‑NSSAI, it may select one based on operator configuration or defer the selection until a NF/service within the slice is needed. (TS 23.501, §5.15.5.2.1)  
* Determines the target AMF Set or, based on configuration, the list of candidate AMFs, possibly after querying the NRF. (TS 23.501, §5.15.5.2.1)  

These actions together enable the NSSF to guide slice selection, AMF assignment, and slice‑replacement handling for the UE.

A QoS Flow is the finest granularity of QoS differentiation in a PDU Session; it is identified by a QoS Flow ID (QFI) that is unique within the PDU Session and is used to apply the same forwarding treatment (e.g., scheduling, admission thresholds, queue management, rate shaping, RLC configuration) to all user‑plane traffic carrying that QFI. The QoS Flow is controlled by the SMF, may be pre‑configured or established/modified via PDU Session procedures, and is the entity to which a QoS profile, QoS rules and optional QoS parameters are applied. (TS 23.501, §5.7.1.1) (TS 23.501, §3.1)

The Policy Control Function (PCF) is the 5G Core network function that centrally governs policy control. It implements a unified policy framework, provides policy rules to other Control‑Plane functions for enforcement, and accesses subscription information stored in the Unified Data Repository (UDR) to make policy decisions. The PCF also supports PDU‑Set‑based handling and interacts with other network functions (e.g., SMF, UPF, AF, NEF) to apply policies such as access control, mobility management, session management, background data transfer, UE‑policy association, event exposure, and service‑function‑chaining control【TS 23.501, §6.2.4】.

Cause #9 – “UE identity cannot be derived by the network” is a 5GMM cause that is sent to the UE when the network is unable to obtain the UE’s identity from the received 5G‑GUTI or 5G‑S‑TMSI. This may occur because there is no matching identity/context in the network or because an integrity‑check failure prevents validation of the UE’s identity【TS 24.501, §A.1】. When this cause is received, the UE must set the 5GS update status to 5U2 NOT UPDATED, delete any stored 5G‑GUTI, last visited registered TAI, TAI list and ngKSI, and enter the 5GMM‑DEREGISTERED state【TS 24.501, §5.6.1.5】.

Timer **T3510** is a retransmission timer used by the UE during the registration procedure.

* **Value** – The default timer value is **15 seconds** (it is 85 s in WB‑N1/CE mode and 27 s for access via a satellite NG‑RAN cell)【TS 24.501, §10.2】.  

* **When it is started** – T3510 is started **when the UE transmits a REGISTRATION REQUEST message** (i.e., at the beginning of the registration procedure)【TS 24.501, §10.2】.  

* **When it is stopped** –  
  * The timer is stopped **upon receipt of a REGISTRATION ACCEPT or REGISTRATION REJECT message**【TS 24.501, §10.2】.  
  * It is also stopped when the UE aborts the registration procedure (e.g., because the validity information for the selected SNPN is no longer met) and locally releases the NAS signalling connection【TS 24.501, §5.5.1.2.7】.  
  * Additionally, the UE stops T3510 when it detects an authentication failure and sends an AUTHENTICATION FAILURE message; in that case the UE stops any retransmission timers that are running, including T3510【TS 24.501, §5.4.1.2.4.5】.  

Thus, T3510 is a 15‑second retransmission timer started with the transmission of a REGISTRATION REQUEST and stopped either by a successful or rejected registration response, by aborting the registration procedure, or by an authentication‑failure handling.

The REGISTRATION REQUEST message includes the following **mandatory** information elements (IEs) — each marked “M” in the specification:

* Extended protocol discriminator (IEI – 9.2)【TS 24.501, §8.2.6.1】  
* Security header type (IEI – 9.3)【TS 24.501, §8.2.6.1】  
* Spare half octet (IEI – 9.5)【TS 24.501, §8.2.6.1】  
* Registration request message identity (IEI – 9.7)【TS 24.501, §8.2.6.1】  
* 5GS registration type (IEI – 9.11.3.7)【TS 24.501, §8.2.6.1】  
* NAS key set identifier (ngKSI) (IEI – 9.11.3.32)【TS 24.501, §8.2.6.1】  
* 5GS mobile identity (IEI – 9.11.3.4)【TS 24.501, §8.2.6.1】

These are the only IEs that the specification marks as mandatory for the REGISTRATION REQUEST message.

The service request procedure is used to 

* change the UE’s 5GMM mode from 5GMM‑IDLE to 5GMM‑CONNECTED;  
* request establishment of user‑plane resources for PDU sessions that are set up without user‑plane resources when the UE is not using 5GS services with control‑plane CIoT optimisation and the 5GMM mode is 5GMM‑IDLE or 5GMM‑CONNECTED; and  
* initiate transfer of user data via the control plane when the UE is using 5GS services with control‑plane CIoT optimisation and the 5GMM mode is 5GMM‑IDLE.  

(TS 24.501, §5.6.1.1)

5GSM cause #26 indicates “insufficient resources” – it is used by the network (or the UE) to indicate that the requested service or PDU‑session operation cannot be provided because the required resources are not available. (TS 24.501, §B.1) (TS 24.501, §6.4.1.4.1)

The NAS security mode control procedure is used to bring a 5G NAS security context into use and to initialise and start NAS signalling security between the UE and the AMF with the appropriate 5G NAS keys and security algorithms (TS 24.501, §5.4.2.1).

The UE can indicate the following registration types in the **5GS registration type IE**:

* **initial registration** – used for the normal first registration of a UE for 5GS services【TS 24.501, §5.5.1.2.1】  
* **emergency registration** – used when the UE registers for emergency services【TS 24.501, §5.5.1.2.1】  
* **SNPN onboarding registration** – used for the initial registration for onboarding services in a secondary public network (SNPN)【TS 24.501, §5.5.1.2.1】  
* **disaster roaming initial registration** – used for the initial registration for disaster‑roaming services【TS 24.501, §5.5.1.2.1】  
* **mobility registration updating** – used when the UE updates its registration due to mobility (e.g., change of PLMN or tracking area)【TS 24.501, §5.5.1.3.2】  
* **periodic registration updating** – used for periodic registration updates required by the network【TS 24.501, §5.5.1.3.2】

The SMF is the network function that performs the session‑management functions required to provide PDU‑connectivity service to the UE over the 5GSM signalling. It is responsible for the UE‑requested PDU session establishment (as well as authentication, modification and release) and for generating the appropriate NAS SM messages that establish the session [TS 24.501, §6.2.3].

During a UE‑requested establishment the UE sends a **PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT REQUEST** message to the SMF, and the SMF replies with a **PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT ACCEPT** message to indicate that the PDU session has been accepted [TS 24.501, §6.4.1.3].

The UE can leave the registered condition by moving from **RM‑REGISTERED** to **RM‑DEREGISTERED** and by exchanging the NAS de‑registration messages defined in TS 24.501.

**RM‑REGISTERED → RM‑DEREGISTERED**

* The UE may initiate a deregistration at any time (e.g., by sending a DEREGISTRATION REQUEST) and the network may also decide to deregister the UE at any time【1†L9-L12】【3†L1-L4】.  
* When the UE initiates the procedure, it performs the **Deregistration procedure** (see clause 4.2.2.3.1 of TS 23.502) and, after the network’s response, the UE enters **RM‑DEREGISTERED**【1†L13-L16】.  
* If the UE receives a **Registration Reject** or a **Deregistration** message from the network, it also enters **RM‑DEREGISTERED**【1†L17-L19】.  
* The AMF, when its UE RM state is **RM‑REGISTERED**, can also trigger deregistration and will change the UE’s state to **RM‑DEREGISTERED** after completing the procedure【1†L20-L22】.  
* After the UE is in **RM‑DEREGISTERED**, it is not registered with the PLMN and holds no valid location or routing information in the AMF【5†L1-L4】. The UE may later perform an Initial Registration to return to **RM‑REGISTERED**【5†L5-L9】.

**NAS de‑registration messages**

* The UE sends a **DEREGISTRATION REQUEST** message to the network to start the procedure.  
* Upon successful completion, the UE shall send a **DEREGISTRATION ACCEPT** message and enter the NAS state **5GMM‑DEREGISTERED** (for both 3GPP and non‑3GPP access)【2†L1-L3】【4†L1-L3】.  
* If the network’s DEREGISTRATION REQUEST indicates “re‑registration not required” for non‑3GPP access, the UE performs a local release of the relevant PDU sessions before sending DEREGISTRATION ACCEPT【4†L4-L9】.  
* In abnormal cases where the N1 NAS signalling connection is lost before the UE receives DEREGISTRATION ACCEPT, the de‑registration procedure is aborted and the UE enters **5GMM‑NULL** (if de‑registration was due to disabling 5GS services) or **5GMM‑DEREGISTERED** (for normal de‑registration)【6†L1-L7】.  

Thus, deregistration consists of a transition from **RM‑REGISTERED** to **RM‑DEREGISTERED** (initiated by the UE or the network) together with the exchange of the NAS **DEREGISTRATION REQUEST** and **DEREGISTRATION ACCEPT** messages, after which the UE is in the NAS state **5GMM‑DEREGISTERED**.

Network slicing is identified in the 5G system by the **S‑NSSAI (Single Network Slice Selection Assistance Information)**, which is used to represent each network slice (or slice instance) of the HPLMN or SNPN [1].  

During the registration procedure the UE indicates the slices it wants by including a **Requested NSSAI** in the Registration Request message. The Requested NSSAI contains the S‑NSSAIs that the UE wishes to use and, when the request is based on the Default Configured NSSAI, the UE shall indicate this in the Registration Request [1]. The UE may also signal support for network‑slice related features (e.g., network‑controlled Slice Usage Policy or temporarily available slices) in the **UE MM Core Network Capability** IE of the Registration Request [2][6].

A UE that is in **CM‑IDLE** initiates a Service Request procedure when it needs to establish a NAS signalling connection, for example  

* when it receives a paging request, or  
* when it has uplink signalling or user data to send (including high‑priority or emergency cases)【5†§5.3.3.2.2】.  

The procedure is started by the UE sending a **SERVICE REQUEST** NAS message to the AMF【2†§5.6.1.2.1】.

A **QoS flow** is identified by a QoS Flow Identifier (QFI) and is associated with a set of QoS parameters (e.g., 5QI, GBR, MBR, averaging window) that are signalled to the UE together with the QoS rule(s) that refer to that flow (TS 23.501, §5.7.1.5).  

A **QoS rule** that is signalled to the UE contains the following elements (TS 24.501, §9.11.4.13 and TS 23.501, §5.7.1.4):  

* a **QoS rule identifier** (unique within the PDU Session) – optional; value 0 indicates “no identifier” (TS 24.501, §9.11.4.13, Table 9.11.4.13.1).  
* a **precedence value** that determines the order in which the UE evaluates the rule (higher numeric value → lower precedence) (TS 24.501, §9.11.4.13).  
* a **segregation bit** (in UE‑to‑network direction) indicating whether the UE requests a dedicated QoS flow (TS 24.501, §9.11.4.13).  
* the **QoS flow identifier (QFI)** that binds the rule to a specific QoS flow (TS 24.501, §9.11.4.13).  
* a **Packet Filter Set** (zero or more UL and/or DL packet filters) that defines how user‑plane packets are classified and mapped to the QoS flow (TS 23.501, §5.7.1.4; TS 24.501, §9.11.4.13).  

Thus, a signalled QoS rule conveys the QFI of the associated QoS flow, its identifier, precedence, optional segregation request, and the packet filter set used for traffic classification and marking.

The periodic registration update is used to periodically notify the network of the UE’s availability (i.e., to inform the network that the UE is still reachable) over 3GPP access【2†TS 24.501, §5.3.7】.  
The UE starts this procedure when its periodic registration update timer, T3512, expires【1†TS 24.501, §5.5.1.3.1】.

MICO (Mobile Initiated Connection‑Only) mode is a 5G‑MM feature that allows the UE to operate without the network having to initiate the establishment of an N1 NAS signalling connection; the UE may initiate the connection only when it has data to send [§5.3.6, “Mobile initiated connection only mode”].

The UE can request the use of MICO mode **during a registration procedure** (initial registration, mobility or periodic registration update) by including the **MICO indication IE** in the REGISTRATION REQUEST message [§5.3.6, “Mobile initiated connection only mode”]. The request must be made over a 3GPP access and must not be sent in the situations listed in the same clause (e.g., not during initial registration for emergency services, not when an emergency PDU session is already established, etc.) [§5.3.6, “Mobile initiated connection only mode”].

If the UE also wants to suggest a specific registration timer, it may include the **Requested T3512 value IE** (and optionally an active‑time value) together with the MICO indication IE in the REGISTRATION REQUEST [§5.3.6, “Mobile initiated connection only mode”]. The network then decides whether to accept the request and, if accepted, returns a MICO indication IE in the REGISTRATION ACCEPT message [§5.3.6, “Mobile initiated connection only mode”].

The Network Repository Function (NRF) is the logical function in the 5G Core that stores and manages the profiles of all Network Functions (NFs) and Service Communication Proxies (SCPs) and provides discovery and notification services for them. It maintains the NF and SCP profiles, their supported services, health status, and endpoint addresses, and it answers NF‑Discovery requests from NFs or SCPs by returning the information of the discovered NF instances. In addition, the NRF notifies subscribed consumers about newly registered, updated, or deregistered NF/SCP instances and their services. These capabilities enable other NFs to discover the required NF type or service, either locally configured or via the NRF, and to obtain the appropriate endpoint information for communication【TS 23.501, §6.2.6.1】.  

The NRF also supports service discovery of its own services and endpoint addresses through the NRF bootstrapping service, and it can be deployed at PLMN, shared‑slice, or slice‑specific levels, as well as in visited and home PLMNs for roaming scenarios【TS 23.501, §6.2.6.1】.

The Access and Mobility Management Function (AMF) provides a wide range of core‑network functions, including:

- Termination of the RAN control‑plane interface (N2) and of the NAS interface (N1) together with NAS ciphering and integrity protection.  
- Registration management, connection management, reachability management and mobility management.  
- Lawful intercept for AMF events and the interface to the lawful‑intercept system.  
- Transport of SM (Session Management) messages between the UE and the SMF, acting as a transparent proxy for routing those messages.  
- Access authentication and access authorization.  
- Transport of SMS messages between the UE and the SMSF.  
- Security Anchor Functionality (SEAF) as defined in TS 33.501.  
- Location Services management for regulatory services and transport of Location Services messages between the UE, the LMF and the RAN.  
- EPS Bearer ID allocation for interworking with EPS.  
- UE mobility‑event notification and S‑NSSAI‑per‑TA mapping notification.  
- Support for Control‑Plane CIoT 5GS optimisation and User‑Plane CIoT 5GS optimisation.  
- Support for restriction of use of Enhanced Coverage.  
- Provisioning of external parameters (Expected UE Behaviour parameters or Network Configuration parameters).  
- Support for network‑slice‑specific authentication and authorization.  
- Support for charging.  
- Control of the 5G access‑stratum‑based time distribution based on the UE’s subscription data and control of the gNB’s time‑synchronisation status reporting and subscription.  

These functions are listed in TS 23.501, §6.2.1 (AMF)【TS 23.501, §6.2.1】.
The N4 reference point connects the **SMF (Session Management Function)** and the **UPF (User Plane Function)**【TS 23.501, §4.2.7】.

A 5QI (5G QoS Identifier) is a scalar that is used as a reference to a specific set of 5G QoS characteristics (e.g., scheduling weights, admission thresholds, queue management thresholds, link‑layer protocol configuration, etc.) which determine the forwarding treatment for a QoS Flow. It is not signalled on any interface for standardized values, but it is carried in the QFI field of the N3 tunnel header to associate each PDU with the corresponding QoS Flow (TS 23.501, §5.7.2.1).  

The 5QI therefore serves as a reference to the QoS forwarding behaviour (such as packet loss rate, packet delay budget) that shall be applied to all traffic mapped to the same 5G QoS Flow (TS 23.501, §3.1).

The S‑NSSAI consists of a **Slice/Service Type (SST)** and, optionally, a **Slice Differentiator (SD)**. It is carried as a type‑4 information element whose length is a minimum of 3 octets and a maximum of 10 octets (TS 24.501, §9.11.2.8) and is defined as “comprised of a slice/service type (SST) … and a slice differentiator (SD), inclusion of an SD is optional” (TS 24.501, §4.6.1).

The 5G System defines three Session and Service Continuity (SSC) modes:

* **SSC mode 1** – the network preserves the connectivity service (including the IP address for IPv4/IPv6/IPv4v6 sessions) (TS 23.501, §5.6.9.1).  
* **SSC mode 2** – the network may release the connectivity service and the associated PDU Session(s), causing the allocated IP address(es) to be released (TS 23.501, §5.6.9.1).  
* **SSC mode 3** – the network establishes a new PDU Session Anchor before releasing the previous one, allowing continuity without loss of connectivity (the IP address is not preserved when the anchor changes) (TS 23.501, §5.6.9.1).

The Policy Control Function (PCF) is the network function that centralises policy control in the 5G core. It provides a unified policy framework that governs network behaviour and supplies policy rules to the control‑plane functions so that they can be enforced. To make policy decisions, the PCF accesses subscription information stored in a Unified Data Repository (UDR) located in the same PLMN. It also supports PDU‑Set‑based handling and can control service‑function‑chaining and other traffic‑steering functions as defined in the specifications【TS 23.501, §6.2.4】.  

In addition, the PCF participates in NAS procedures by delivering UE policy information to the UE and by interacting with the AMF, SMF and other network functions as part of both mobility management and session management【TS 24.501, §1】.

The SMF is the network function that performs the session‑management functions that give the UE its PDU‑connectivity service. It is responsible for the UE‑requested PDU session establishment (as well as authentication, modification and release) and for selecting the appropriate parameters (e.g., S‑NSSAI, PDU‑session type, address allocation) that are conveyed to the UE in the establishment response (TS 24.501, §6.2.3).  

During a UE‑requested establishment the UE sends a **PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT REQUEST** message to the SMF (via the AMF), and the SMF replies with a **PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT ACCEPT** message when the procedure is accepted (TS 24.501, §6.4.1.3).

The UE can leave the registered state by performing a **Deregistration procedure**.  

**RM‑REGISTERED → RM‑DEREGISTERED**  
* When the UE decides that it no longer needs to be registered, it initiates the deregistration procedure (or the network may request it) and, after the procedure is completed, the UE shall be in the **RM‑DEREGISTERED** state (TS 23.501, §5.3.2.2.3).  
* The AMF also may trigger deregistration; after the AMF’s deregistration actions the UE is placed in RM‑DEREGISTERED (TS 23.501, §5.3.2.2.3).  

**NAS signalling**  
* The UE sends a **DEREGISTRATION REQUEST** NAS message to the AMF to start the procedure.  
* When the network (or the UE, in the case of a network‑initiated request) completes the procedure, the UE shall send a **DEREGISTRATION ACCEPT** NAS message and then enter the 5GMM‑DEREGISTERED state (TS 24.501, §5.5.2.3.2).  

**Resulting 5GMM state**  
* After sending DEREGISTRATION ACCEPT, the UE is in **5GMM‑DEREGISTERED** for the relevant access (3GPP or non‑3GPP) (TS 24.501, §5.5.2.3.2).  

Thus, deregistration moves the UE from RM‑REGISTERED to RM‑DEREGISTERED, and the NAS exchange that finalises the process consists of a DEREGISTRATION REQUEST followed by a DEREGISTRATION ACCEPT, after which the UE is in the 5GMM‑DEREGISTERED state.

Network slicing is identified in the 5G architecture by the **Single Network Slice Selection Assistance Information (S‑NSSAI)**, which is carried in the UE’s **Network Slice Selection Assistance Information (NSSAI)** for the serving PLMN. The S‑NSSAI values are used by the (R)AN and the AMF to select the appropriate network slice instance for the UE (TS 23.501, §5.15.5.2.1).

During the registration procedure the UE includes the **Requested NSSAI** in the NAS Registration Request message. The Requested NSSAI contains the S‑NSSAI(s) that the UE wishes to use and indicates whether the request is based on the Default Configured NSSAI. The UE shall only include a Requested NSSAI when it has a Configured NSSAI, an Allowed NSSAI, or the Default Configured NSSAI for the PLMN and Access Type (TS 23.501, §5.15.5.2.1). This Requested NSSAI is also carried in the RRC Connection Establishment and, when applicable, in the connection establishment to the N3IWF/TNGF (TS 23.501, §5.15.5.2.1).

A UE that is in **CM‑IDLE** initiates a **Service Request** procedure when it receives a paging request or when it has uplink signalling or user‑data to send (unless it is in MICO mode or otherwise restricted)【TS 23.501, §5.3.3.2.2】.  

The NAS signalling that starts the procedure is the **SERVICE REQUEST** message sent by the UE to the AMF【TS 24.501, §5.6.1.2.1】.

The periodic registration update is the procedure that the UE uses to periodically inform the network of its availability (i.e., to notify the network that the UE is still reachable) over 3GPP access【3†TS 24.501, §5.3.7】.  
The UE starts this procedure when its periodic registration update timer, T3512, expires【1†TS 24.501, §5.5.1.3.1】.

MICO (Mobile‑Initiated Connection Only) mode is a UE operation mode in which the UE is considered unreachable by the network while it is in the AMF CM‑IDLE state; down‑link data or signalling is only delivered when the UE is in CM‑CONNECTED, and the UE does not have to listen to paging while in CM‑IDLE【TS 23.501, §5.4.1.3】. In MICO mode the UE may stop all access‑stratum procedures in CM‑IDLE and will only transition to CM‑CONNECTED when a trigger such as a change in configuration, periodic registration timer expiry, pending MO data or pending MO signalling occurs【TS 23.501, §5.4.1.3】.

The UE requests the use of MICO mode by including the **MICO indication Information Element** in the NAS **REGISTRATION REQUEST** message. If the UE does not include this IE, the AMF shall disable MICO mode if it was previously enabled【TS 24.501, §5.5.1.3.4】. The AMF then decides whether to accept the request and, if accepted, enables MICO mode for the UE.

The Policy Control Function (PCF) is the 5G Core network function that governs network behaviour through a unified policy framework. The SMF is the network function that carries out the session‑management procedures for a PDU session. It is responsible for the PDU‑connectivity service to the UE, for checking that the UE’s request complies with the subscription (e.g., allowed PDU‑session types, QoS, security policy), for interacting with the UDM to obtain subscription data, and for configuring the UPF (ATSSS/N4 rules) as part of the establishment (TS 24.501, §6.2.3).  

During a UE‑requested PDU‑session establishment the UE sends a **PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT REQUEST** message to the SMF (via the AMF), and the SMF replies with a **PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT ACCEPT** message when the session can be set up (TS 24.501, §6.4.1.3).

A UE that is in **CM‑IDLE** initiates a Service Request procedure when it has to respond to a paging request or when it has uplink signalling or user‑data to send (i.e. when the UE needs to establish a NAS signalling connection). In this situation the UE sends a **SERVICE REQUEST** NAS message to the AMF, which starts the procedure【TS 23.501, §5.3.3.2.2】.

QoS flows are identified by a **QoS Flow Identifier (QFI)**, which is carried in the QoS rule and is used by the UE and the network to bind user‑plane packets to a specific QoS Flow (TS 24.501, §9.11.4.13). The QFI may be associated with a set of QoS Flow‑level parameters (e.g., 5QI, GBR, MBR, averaging window) that are signalled to the UE together with the QoS rule(s) (TS 23.501, §5.7.1.5).

A QoS rule that is signalled to the UE contains the following elements:

* **QoS rule identifier** – a value unique within the PDU Session (0 … 255, with 0 meaning “no identifier”) (TS 24.501, §9.11.4.13, Table 9.11.4.13.1).  
* **QoS rule precedence** – a binary‑coded value (0 … 255) that determines the order in which the UE evaluates the rule; a higher numeric value means lower precedence (TS 24.501, §9.11.4.13).  
* **Segregation bit** – indicates whether the UE requests the network to bind the service data flows described by the rule to a dedicated QoS Flow (TS 24.501, §9.11.4.13).  
* **QoS flow identifier (QFI)** – the identifier of the QoS Flow to which matching packets are bound (TS 24.501, §9.11.4.13).  
* **Packet Filter Set** – zero or more UL and/or DL packet filters that define how user‑plane packets are classified and mapped to the QoS Flow (TS 24.501, §9.11.4.13).  
* For explicitly signalled rules, the **QoS rule identifier** is generated by the SMF and is unique within the session (TS 23.501, §5.7.1.4).  

Thus, a signalled QoS rule conveys the identifier, precedence, segregation request, QFI, and the set of packet filters that together enable the UE to classify, mark, and bind traffic to the corresponding QoS Flow.

A QoS Flow is the finest granularity of QoS differentiation within a PDU Session; it is identified by a QoS Flow ID (QFI) that is unique per PDU Session and carried in the N3/N9 encapsulation header, and it determines the traffic‑forwarding treatment (e.g., scheduling, admission thresholds) applied to user‑plane traffic sharing the same QFI (TS 23.501, §5.7.1.1).

* provides a unified policy framework that governs overall network behaviour, 
* supplies policy rules to other Control‑Plane functions so that they can be enforced, 
* retrieves the subscription information needed for policy decisions from the Unified Data Repository (UDR), and 
* supports PDU‑Set‑based handling as defined in clause 5.37.5 (TS 23.501, §6.2.4)【1】.  

In addition, the PCF offers a set of NF services (e.g., Npcf_AMPolicyControl, Npcf_SMPolicyControl, Npcf_UEPolicyControl, etc.) that deliver access‑control, mobility‑management, session‑related, and UE‑policy‑association policies to consuming network functions (TS 23.501, §7.2.4)【6】.

Cause #9 – UE identity cannot be derived by the network. This 5GMM cause is sent to the UE when the network cannot derive the UE’s identity from the 5G‑GUTI or 5G‑S‑TMSI because, for example, there is no matching identity/context in the network or an integrity‑check failure of the received message prevents validation of the UE’s identity (TS 24.501, §A.1).

Timer **T3510** is a 5GS mobility‑management timer used on the UE side.

* **Value** – 15 seconds (with special notes for other modes, e.g., 85 s in WB‑N1/CE mode and 27 s for satellite NG‑RAN access) (TS 24.501, §10.2).  
* **When it is started** – The timer is started **at registration failure** when the UE is in the *5GMM‑REGISTERED‑INITIATED* state, i.e., when a **REGISTRATION REQUEST** message is transmitted (TS 24.501, §10.2).  
* **When it is stopped (normal stop)** – The timer stops when the UE receives either a **REGISTRATION ACCEPT** message or a **REGISTRATION REJECT** message (TS 24.501, §10.2).

The SMF is the network function that performs the session‑management functions required to give the UE a PDU‑connectivity service. It carries out the procedures for establishing, authenticating, authorising, modifying and releasing a PDU session and therefore provides the PDU connectivity service to the UE over the 5GSM signalling between the UE and the SMF (TS 24.501, §6.2.3).  

During the establishment of a PDU session the UE (via the AMF) sends a **PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT REQUEST** message to the SMF. If the SMF accepts the request it returns a **PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT ACCEPT** message (the counterpart of the request) to the UE (TS 24.501, §6.4.1.7, d‑f).  

Thus, the SMF’s role is to manage the PDU session establishment procedure, and the 5GSM messages used for the request and acceptance are the PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT REQUEST and PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT ACCEPT.

The UE can deregister from the PLMN by executing the **Deregistration procedure** defined for the RM‑REGISTERED state.  
When the UE decides that it no longer needs to be registered, it initiates the Deregistration procedure (see clause 4.2.2.3.1 of TS 23.502) and, after the procedure is completed, the UE **enters the RM‑DEREGISTERED state** (TS 23.501, §5.3.2.2.3)【3†L9-L12】.  

In the RM‑DEREGISTERED state the UE is not registered with the network; it may later start an Initial Registration procedure if it needs service again, or it remains in this state if a Registration Reject is received (TS 23.501, §5.3.2.2.2)【5†L1-L7】.  

The specification also states that the **network may decide to deregister the UE at any time** and, after an implicit deregistration timer expires, the AMF shall move the UE to the RM‑DEREGISTERED state (TS 23.501, §5.3.2.2.3)【1†L1-L4】.

Network slicing is identified in the 5G system by the **S‑NSSAI (Single Network Slice Selection Assistance Information)**, which is used in the Configured NSSAI, Allowed NSSAI and Requested NSSAI lists exchanged between the UE and the AMF (see §5.15.12.2 “UE and UE configuration aspects”) (TS 23.501, §5.15.12.2).  

During the Registration procedure the UE indicates the slices it wants to use by including the **Requested NSSAI** IE in the Registration Request message. The UE may also indicate support for features such as network‑controlled Slice Usage Policy or subscription‑based restrictions to simultaneous registration of network slices in the **UE 5GMM Core Network Capability** IE (see §5.15.15.2 and §5.15.12.2) (TS 23.501, §5.15.15.2; TS 23.501, §5.15.12.2).  

If the UE supports network‑controlled Slice Usage Policy, the AMF can provide a Slice Usage Policy together with the Configured NSSAI in the Registration Accept, allowing the UE to register on‑demand slices or to use a slice deregistration inactivity timer (see §5.15.15.2) (TS 23.501, §5.15.15.2).  

Thus, network slicing is identified by S‑NSSAI values, and the UE signals the desired slices in the Requested NSSAI IE of the Registration Request, optionally indicating support for related capabilities in the UE 5GMM Core Network Capability.

A UE that is in **CM‑IDLE** initiates a Service Request procedure in two situations:

* **When the UE receives paging** while it is also in RM‑REGISTERED state, it shall respond by performing a Service Request procedure (unless it is in MICO mode)【TS 23.501, §5.3.3.2.2】.  
* **When the UE has uplink signalling or user data to send**, it shall also perform a Service Request procedure【TS 23.501, §5.3.3.2.2】.

The NAS message that starts the procedure is the **SERVICE REQUEST** message sent by the UE【TS 23.501, §5.3.3.2.2】.

QoS flows are identified by a **QoS Flow Identifier (QFI)** and are associated with the QoS parameters that the network has derived for the flow (e.g., 5QI, guaranteed‑bit‑rate (GFBR), maximum‑bit‑rate (MFBR), averaging‑window, etc.) as well as the packet‑marking information (e.g., the QFI itself and the transport‑level marking value such as the DSCP of the outer IP header). When a PCC rule is bound to a QoS Flow, the SMF may generate an explicitly signalled QoS rule for that flow and provide it to the UE【5†L1-L7】.  

A QoS rule that is signalled to the UE contains the following elements:

* **QoS rule identifier** – a unique identifier for the rule within the PDU session (or “no QoS rule identifier assigned” when not used)【2†L1-L7】.  
* **QoS rule precedence** – the precedence value of the rule (higher numeric value means lower precedence)【2†L9-L15】.  
* **Segregation bit** – indicates whether the UE requests a dedicated QoS Flow for the service data flows described by the rule【2†L17-L23】.  
* **QoS flow identifier (QFI)** – the QFI of the QoS Flow to which the rule is bound【2†L25-L31】.  
* **Packet Filter Set** – a set of packet filters generated from the UL (and optionally DL) SDF filters of the bound PCC rule, used for classification and marking of uplink traffic【5†L9-L13】.  

Thus, a QoS rule signalled to the UE carries the rule identifier, precedence, segregation indication, the QFI of the associated QoS Flow, and the packet‑filter set that defines how UL traffic is classified and marked.

The periodic registration update procedure is used by the UE to periodically notify the network of its availability (i.e., to inform the network that the UE is still reachable) [TS 24.501, §5.3.7].  
The UE starts this procedure when its periodic registration update timer, T3512, expires [TS 24.501, §5.5.1.3.1].

MICO (Mobile‑initiated Connection‑Only) mode is a NAS operation in which the UE is allowed to keep the AS layer de‑activated and only initiate signalling or user‑data transfer when it explicitly decides to reactivate the AS layer. While MICO mode is active the UE does not establish a NAS signalling connection for routine registration, tracking‑area update or periodic registration procedures, and it may only deactivate MICO mode when it needs to send mobile‑originated signalling or data (or when an emergency PDU session is established)【5†L1-L4】.  

The UE requests the use of MICO mode during a registration procedure (initial registration, registration update or periodic registration update) by including the **MICO indication IE** in the registration request message. The request may also contain an **active time value** (in T3324 IE) and, if the UE wishes a specific value for the periodic monitoring timer, a **Requested T3512 value IE**【1†L1-L9】. The network can accept the request by returning the MICO indication IE in the registration accept message. If the network accepts MICO mode without an active time value, it may include an “all PLMN registration area allocated” indication in the same IE【1†L10-L12】.  

Thus, the UE signals its desire to operate in MICO mode by sending the MICO indication IE (optionally with active‑time and Requested T3512 IEs) in the NAS registration request.

The Network Repository Function (NRF) is the central repository that maintains information about all Network Functions (NFs) and Service Communication Proxies (SCPs) in the 5G Core. It stores NF profiles, the services they offer, their endpoint addresses, health status and slice‑related information, and it provides service‑discovery functions so that other CP NFs or SCPs can locate NF instances that provide the required services. The NRF also supports discovery of specialized services such as P‑CSCF (via SMF) and notifies subscribed consumers about newly registered, updated or deregistered NF/SCP instances. (TS 23.501, §6.2.1) 

In addition, the NRF can be deployed at different hierarchical levels (PLMN, shared‑slice, slice‑specific) and, in roaming scenarios, separate NRFs exist in the visited and home PLMNs that inter‑connect via the N27 interface. (TS 23.501, §6.2.1)

A 5QI (5‑G QoS Identifier) is a scalar value that serves as a reference to the 5G QoS characteristics applied to a QoS Flow. It identifies a specific set of forwarding treatment parameters (such as scheduling weights, admission thresholds, queue management thresholds, and link‑layer protocol configuration) that are used edge‑to‑edge between the UE and the UPF. The 5QI itself does not carry the QoS characteristics on the interfaces; instead, the value points to either standardized or pre‑configured characteristics defined in the specifications【TS 23.501, §5.7.2.1】.  

In the terminology of the specifications, the 5QI is defined as “a scalar that is used as a reference to a specific QoS forwarding behaviour (e.g. packet loss rate, packet delay budget) to be provided to a 5G QoS Flow”【TS 23.501, §3.1】.

An S‑NSSAI consists of a **Slice/Service Type (SST)** and, optionally, a **Slice Differentiator (SD)**. The SST identifies the expected network‑slice behaviour, while the SD (when present) further distinguishes among multiple slices of the same SST [TS 23.501, §5.15.2.1].  

In the access‑stratum signalling the S‑NSSAI is carried as a type‑4 information element whose length is a minimum of 3 octets and a maximum of 10 octets, reflecting the presence of the mandatory SST and the optional SD [TS 24.501, §9.11.2.8].

The 5G System defines three Service and Session Continuity (SSC) modes:

* **SSC mode 1** – the network preserves the connectivity service (e.g., the IP address is retained for IPv4/IPv6 PDU Sessions).  
* **SSC mode 2** – the network may release the connectivity service and the associated PDU Session(s), causing the allocated IP address(es) to be released.  
* **SSC mode 3** – the user‑plane change is visible to the UE, but the network ensures no loss of connectivity by establishing a new PDU Session Anchor before terminating the previous one; the IP address is not preserved when the anchor changes.  

These three modes are specified in the specification (TS 23.501, §5.6.9.1)【TS 23.501, §5.6.9.1】.

The Network Slice Selection Function (NSSF) is responsible for the selection and management of network slices for a UE. Its main duties are:

* Selecting the set of Network Slice instances that will serve the UE and determining the Allowed and Configured NSSAI, including any mapping to the Subscribed S‑NSSAIs (TS 23.501, §6.2.14).  
* Determining which AMF Set (or list of candidate AMFs) should be used for the UE, possibly after querying the NRF (TS 23.501, §5.15.5.2.1).  
* Using locally available information (e.g., RAN capabilities, load level, NWDAF analytics) to verify the Requested NSSAI against the Subscribed S‑NSSAIs, to select permitted S‑NSSAIs, and to choose the appropriate Network Slice instance(s) (TS 23.501, §5.15.5.2.1).  
* Providing support for Network Slice restriction and Network Slice instance restriction based on NWDAF analytics (TS 23.501, §6.2.14).  
* Detecting when an S‑NSSAI becomes unavailable or congested and sending a network‑slice‑availability notification to the AMF, optionally including an Alternative S‑NSSAI and congestion‑mitigation information (TS 23.501, §5.15.19).  
* Supporting Network Slice Replacement by indicating that an S‑NSSAI is unavailable and supplying an Alternative S‑NSSAI, based on NWDAF analytics or OAM triggers (TS 23.501, §6.2.14).  
* Supplying, when required, an NSI‑ID to be used for NF selection within the selected Network Slice instance (TS 23.501, §5.15.5.3).  

In summary, the NSSF selects appropriate slices and AMF sets for a UE, validates and maps S‑NSSAIs, leverages analytics for load‑aware decisions, and handles slice‑unavailability or congestion by notifying the AMF and providing alternative slice information.

Initial registration is the procedure by which a UE is first registered with the 5G Core. During this procedure the AMF creates the UE’s registration state, stores the UE’s capability information, and assigns a Tracking Area Identity (TAI) list that defines the registration area of the UE (TS 24.501, §5.5.1.2.4).  

To carry out the initial registration the UE sends a **REGISTRATION REQUEST** message to the AMF, and, if the request is accepted, the AMF replies with a **REGISTRATION ACCEPT** message that contains the assigned TAI list (TS 24.501, §5.5.1.2.4).  

Thus, the NAS message exchange that implements the initial registration consists of the UE‑to‑AMF **REGISTRATION REQUEST** and the AMF‑to‑UE **REGISTRATION ACCEPT**. (TS 24.501, §5.5.1.2.4)

The SMF performs the session‑management functions that provide the PDU‑connectivity service to the UE. It is responsible for the PDU‑session establishment (as well as modification and release) procedures and for allocating and managing the UE IP address, selecting and controlling the UPF, and configuring traffic steering for the session【1†L1-L6】.  

During a UE‑requested PDU‑session establishment the UE sends a **PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT REQUEST** message (carried over the N1 NAS signalling via the AMF) to the SMF, and the SMF replies with a **PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT ACCEPT** message (also transferred via the AMF) when the establishment is accepted【4†L1-L4】【6†L1-L4】.

A UE deregisters from the network by executing the **Deregistration procedure** defined in the NAS layer and by moving its registration‑management (RM) state from **RM‑REGISTERED** to **RM‑DEREGISTERED**.

* **RM‑REGISTERED → RM‑DEREGISTERED** – When the UE decides that it no longer wants to be registered, it initiates the deregistration procedure (clause 4.2.2.3.1 of TS 23.502) and, after the procedure is completed, the UE shall enter the RM‑DEREGISTERED state (TS 23.501, §5.3.2.2.3). The network can also cause the UE to deregister at any time, for example by performing an implicit deregistration after the implicit‑deregistration timer expires, after which the AMF places the UE in RM‑DEREGISTERED (TS 23.501, §5.3.2.2.3).  

* **NAS signalling** – The UE starts the deregistration by sending a **DEREGISTRATION REQUEST** NAS message to the AMF. If the lower‑layer N1 NAS signalling connection is released before the UE receives a **DEREGISTRATION ACCEPT**, the deregistration procedure is aborted and the UE either enters 5GMM‑NULL (if the deregistration was due to disabling of 5GS services) or re‑enters 5GMM‑DEREGISTERED (if it was a normal deregistration) (TS 24.501, §5.5.2.2.6). When the DEREGISTRATION ACCEPT is received, the UE may locally release the N1 NAS signalling connection (if timer T3540 is not running) and then moves to the appropriate 5GMM‑DEREGISTERED sub‑state (TS 24.501, §5.3.1.3).  

Thus, deregistration consists of the UE sending a DEREGISTRATION REQUEST, handling the possible ACCEPT or abort conditions as defined in the NAS procedures, and consequently transitioning its RM state from RM‑REGISTERED to RM‑DEREGISTERED.

Network slicing is identified in the signalling architecture by the **Network slicing indication** information element, which is defined as a type‑1 IE and is used in the generic UE configuration update and registration procedures to convey additional network‑slicing related information beyond the NSSAI lists (TS 24.501, §9.11.3.36)【2】. This IE must be present in a Registration Request when the UE’s Requested NSSAI is derived from the default configured NSSAI (TS 24.501, §8.2.6.19)【6】.  

During the Registration procedure the UE indicates the slices it wishes to register to by including a **Requested NSSAI** in the NAS message. The Requested NSSAI contains the S‑NSSAI(s) of the Network Slice(s) the UE wants to register for, and it may be the default configured NSSAI, a subset of the Configured‑NSSAI, the Allowed‑NSSAI for the access type, or a combination thereof as defined in the registration rules (TS 23.501, §5.15.5.2.1)【3】.

A UE that is in **CM‑IDLE** (i.e., has no NAS signalling connection with the AMF) shall initiate a Service Request procedure:

* **When paging is received** – the UE responds to the paging by performing a Service Request (unless it is in MICO mode)【TS 23.501, §5.3.3.2.2】.  
* **When the UE has uplink signalling or user data to send** – the UE also performs a Service Request (with specific conditions for LADN)【TS 23.501, §5.3.3.2.2】.

The NAS message that starts this procedure is the **SERVICE REQUEST** message sent by the UE to the AMF【TS 24.501, §5.6.1.2.1】.

A **QoS Flow** is an entity that carries user‑plane traffic with a set of QoS requirements (QoS parameters and QoS characteristics). Within a PDU Session a default QoS Flow (non‑GBR) must always be established and remains active for the whole session lifetime; additional QoS Flows can be created and are associated with one or more QoS rules that the SMF provides to the UE (TS 23.501, §5.7.1.1). The QoS Flow may also be derived by the UE through Reflective QoS control (TS 23.501, §5.7.1.5).  

A **QoS rule** signalled to the UE contains:

* a unique QoS‑rule identifier for the PDU Session,  
* the precedence value (taken from the PCC rule that generated the QoS rule),  
* the QFI that identifies the associated QoS Flow,  
* a set of packet filters generated from the UL (and optionally DL) SDF filters of the bound PCC rule, and  
* optional information such as the Reflective QoS indication (TS 23.501, §5.7.1.5).  

The QoS‑rules information element itself is defined in TS 24.501 as a type‑6 IE that carries one or more QoS rules, each of which includes the parameters needed for classification and marking of uplink traffic and for identification of the QoS Flow used for downlink traffic (TS 24.501, §9.11.4.13).

The periodic registration update procedure is used to periodically inform the network of the UE’s availability (i.e., to notify the network that the UE is reachable) over 3GPP access【1†L1-L4】.  
The UE starts this procedure when its periodic registration update timer, T3512, expires【3†L9-L12】.

MICO (Mobile Initiated Connection Only) mode is a power‑saving operating mode in which the UE is considered unreachable while it is in the CM‑IDLE state and only becomes reachable when it initiates mobile‑originated (MO) data or signalling or when a periodic registration timer expires. In this mode the UE does not listen to paging and the network rejects down‑link delivery attempts while the UE is CM‑IDLE【3】.

The UE can request the use of MICO mode during a registration procedure (Initial Registration or Mobility Registration Update) by indicating a preference for MICO mode in the registration request. The request is carried in the MICO indication Information Element (IE) and may optionally include an active‑time value (T3324 IE) and a Requested T3512 value IE if the UE wants a specific periodic registration timer value【1】. If the UE does not include a preference for MICO mode, the AMF shall not activate MICO mode for that UE【4】.

The SMF (Session Management Function) is responsible for the session management functions to provide the PDU connectivity service to the UE (User Equipment) via the 5GSM signalling between UE and SMF.

To request a PDU session, the UE sends a PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT REQUEST message to the SMF, which includes the 5GSM capability IE with the RQoS bit set to "Reflective QoS supported" and/or the Maximum number of supported packet filters IE.

To accept a PDU session, the SMF sends a PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT ACCEPT message to the UE, which includes the PDU address IE, the Session-AMBR IE, and other relevant information.

If the selected PDU session type is "IPv4", "IPv6", "IPv4v6", or "Ethernet", and if the PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT REQUEST message includes a 5GSM capability IE with the RQoS bit set to "Reflective QoS supported", the SMF shall consider that reflective QoS is supported for QoS flows belonging to this PDU session and may include the RQ timer IE set to an RQ timer value in the PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT ACCEPT message.

(Citation: TS 24.501, §6.4.1.3)

To deregister from the network, a UE follows these steps:

1. The UE enters the RM-DEREGISTERED state, indicating that it is not registered with the network.
2. The UE sends a DEREGISTRATION REQUEST message to the network, which may indicate "re-registration not required" for non-3GPP access.
3. If the DEREGISTRATION REQUEST message indicates "re-registration not required" and the de-registration request is for non-3GPP access, the UE performs a local release of the PDU sessions over non-3GPP access, if any.
4. The UE sends a DEREGISTRATION ACCEPT message to the network, which indicates that the de-registration procedure has been completed.
5. The UE enters the 5GMM-DEREGISTERED state for non-3GPP access.

For 3GPP access, the UE sends a DEREGISTRATION ACCEPT message to the network and enters the 5GMM-DEREGISTERED state.

Note that the UE may also perform a local de-registration either immediately or after an implementation-dependent time, depending on the lower layer indications.

In terms of NAS messages, the UE sends the following messages:

* DEREGISTRATION REQUEST message to initiate the de-registration procedure
* DEREGISTRATION ACCEPT message to complete the de-registration procedure

If the DEREGISTRATION REQUEST message has not been sent, the UE proceeds as specified for case b. If the DEREGISTRATION REQUEST message has been sent, the UE proceeds as specified for case a.

MICO mode is a mobile initiated connection only mode, which allows the UE to request the use of MICO mode during the registration procedure.

The UE requests MICO mode by including the Requested T3512 value IE in the REGISTRATION REQUEST message, along with the Requested T3512 value to be allocated. The UE may also request an active time value together with the MICO mode indication during the registration procedure.

If the network accepts the use of MICO mode, it provides a MICO indication when accepting the registration procedure, which includes the MICO indication IE. The MICO indication IE may include an "all PLMN registration area allocated" indication if the network does not include an active time value in T3324 IE to the UE.

If the network indicates support for strictly periodic registration timer in the MICO indication IE to the UE, the network may include a "strictly periodic registration timer supported" indication in the MICO indication IE to the UE.

(TS 24.501, §5.3.6.1)
